newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean won slumps to new seven-year low.
newsitem.headline: South Korean won slumps to new seven-year low.

text.p: The South Korean won slumped to a new seven-year low against the dollar on Friday on speculative buying of the U.S. currency and despite repeated central bank intervention, dealers said.
Dealers and financial analysts said speculators were betting the central bank was losing its ability to brake the won's slide because of dwindling foreign currency holdings.
The won ended Friday at 897.50 after opening at 894.00. It touched 899.30, its lowest since a market average system was introduced in March 1990.
The Bank of Korea announced foreign exchange reserves of $30 billion at the end of February.
Dealers estimated the reserves were now down to about $25 billion after bouts of dollar selling and dollar supplies to banks.
Many economists believe foreign exchange reserves of $35 billion are appropriate given the nation's monthly import bill of $11 billion.
"A desire among corporates to hold dollars is largely propelling the rise," said Han Sang-choon, an economist at the Daewoo Research Institute, explaining the dollar's strength.
The dollar has gained about six percent on the won since the beginning of this year.
Han said the central bank's power to intervene had weakened due to falling dollar reserves.
"Dollar buying strengthened even further because of the central bank's weakening intervention," a domestic bank dealer said.
In addition to its foreign currency holdings, the Bank of Korea has about $28 billion on deposit at domestic banks.

But dealers said this sum could not be counted in the bank's intervention war chest since any attempt to drain funds from the banking system risked exacerbating an already severe short-term financing crunch among banks.
The won has been under pressure largely because of slumping exports.

The current account deficit rose to $2.45 billion in February from $1.97 billion a year before. The deficit for 1996 was $23.72 billion against $10.06 billion in 1995. It is officially forecast to be $18 billion this year.
Corporate dollar holdings have soared to about $5 billion from $1.5 billion a year earlier as a result of a speculative dollar buying, dealers said.
"The dollar should test the 930 level in May," said Oh Suk-tae, a dealer at Citibank.
Financial analysts said further won weakness could spur inflation by making imports more expensive and adding to the burden of foreign debt repayment.
Interest payments on rising foreign debt, now estimated at more than $100 billion, has become a major part of the current account deficit.
The won's depreciation against the dollar is not helping exports much because the yen is falling even faster.
"South Korea has many export items that should compete with Japanese products. So the merit of the won's fall is small," said Oh of Citibank.
Dealers said the dollar shortage could worsen as the collapse of two big steelmakers this year slowed inflows of foreign funds.
